Content:
Consider the vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] shown in the picture below. The vector [MATH: 2\mathbf{a}] is the vector that has the same direction as [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and a length (magnitude) that is twice the length of [MATH: \mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: |2\mathbf{a}|=2 \cdot |\mathbf{a}|]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/cb19d3515f9dc7b8876f0350e9b96be1]

Content:
On the other hand, [MATH: -1.5\mathbf{a}] is the vector that has the opposite direction to [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and its magnitude is [MATH: 1.5] times the magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{a}]:

Content:
[MATH: |-1.5\mathbf{a}|=1.5 \cdot |\mathbf{a}|]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/86844a9c31a6f8b37f8210426acc9d48]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: 2\mathbf{a}] and [MATH: -1.5\mathbf{a}] are both parallel to [MATH: \mathbf a,] and are parallel to each other.

1. [MATH: \mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{c}]
2. [MATH: \mathbf{e}=2\mathbf{a}]
3. [MATH: \mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{e}]

sections.normalized_html:
• Statement I is false. The vectors [MATH: \mathbf{b}] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}] have different magnitudes. So, [MATH: \mathbf{b} \neq -\mathbf{c}.]

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{e}] are parallel and have the same direction. Also, the magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{e}] is [MATH: 2] times the magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{a}]. So, [MATH: \mathbf{e}=2\mathbf{a}.]

  • Statement III is false. The magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{e}] is greater than the magnitude of [MATH: \mathbf{a}]. So, [MATH: \mathbf{a} \neq 2\mathbf{e}.]

Therefore, only statement II is true.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Determining Whether Two Vectors Are Parallel

Content:
In general, two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are called parallel (or collinear) if there exists a number [MATH: \lambda] such that
[MATH: \mathbf{a} = \lambda \mathbf{b}.]
Sometimes, we'll use a special notation
[MATH: \mathbf{a} \parallel \mathbf{b}]
to denote that [MATH: \mathbf{a}] is parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{b}].

Explanation:
Notice that

[MATH: 7\mathbf{a}+14\mathbf{b}= \dfrac{7}{3} (3\mathbf{a}+6\mathbf{b}),]

Therefore, [MATH: \lambda=\dfrac{7}{3}.]
